content: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Atlantic Philanthropies, and the Norwegian Government have collaborated on this initiative. Injuries have emerged as a significant global cause of mortality and disability. To address this, a structured approach to both prevention and treatment is essential. The Guidelines for Essential Trauma Care aim to promote cost-effective improvements in trauma care systems. These guidelines establish realistic standards for trauma treatment services that can be made accessible to nearly all injured individuals worldwide. They also define the necessary resources, including human resources (such as staffing and training) and physical resources (such as infrastructure, equipment, and supplies), required to ensure such care. By clearly outlining these services and resources, the guidelines aim to strengthen trauma treatment services globally. The fundamental premise of these guidelines is that improvements in organization and planning can enhance trauma treatment services and outcomes for injured individuals with minimal additional costs. The authors have developed resource tables for essential trauma care, detailing the human and physical resources required to provide optimal care for injured patients across various healthcare facilities, from rural health posts staffed by non-physicians to small hospitals with general practitioners, specialist-staffed hospitals, and tertiary care centers. These guidelines also consider the varying resource availability in lowand middle-income countries. The guidelines include recommendations for promoting these standards through training, performance improvement, trauma team organization, and hospital inspections. The resource tables and associated recommendations are based on 2002 gross national income (GNI) per capita classifications: low-income (US $735 or less), lower-middle-income (US $736–2935), upper-middle-income (US $2936–9075), and high-income (US $9076 or more). These recommendations serve as a template to help individual countries organize and strengthen their trauma treatment systems, with the expectation that the template will be adapted to local circumstances. The guidelines were developed in collaboration with the WHO Department of Injuries and Violence Prevention, the Working Group for Essential Trauma Care of the International Association for the Surgery of Trauma and Surgical Intensive Care (IATSIC), other WHO departments, and trauma care clinicians from Africa, Asia, and Latin America. They are primarily directed at healthcare planners and administrators but are also intended for clinicians to advocate for improved trauma care resources. The target audience includes health ministry planners, hospital administrators, nursing service directors, medical service directors, and clinicians, both individually and collectively, through organizations such as surgical, anesthesiology, and traumatology societies. The Essential Trauma Care (EsTC) Project aims to reduce the burden of injury-related death and disability by addressing both prevention and treatment. While prevention offers significant benefits, there are also substantial gains to be made by improving treatment. The EsTC Project identifies and promotes cost-effective ways to enhance trauma treatment worldwide. It focuses on ensuring the availability of these services by strengthening inputs such as human resources (training and staffing) and physical resources (supplies and equipment). These inputs are outlined in a template called the EsTC resource matrix, which serves as a guide for planning trauma treatment services in different countries or regions. The project highlights disparities in trauma outcomes between high-income and lowand middle-income countries. For example, mortality rates for seriously injured adults (injury severity score ≥9) increase from 35% in high-income settings to 55% in middle-income settings and 63% in low-income settings. Among patients who survive to reach the hospital, mortality for moderate-severity injuries (injury severity score 15–24) is six times higher in rural areas of low-income countries compared to hospitals in high-income countries. Additionally, there is a significant burden of disability from extremity injuries in developing countries, which could be mitigated through affordable improvements in orthopedic care and rehabilitation. Improved survival and functional outcomes in high-income countries are often attributed to high-cost equipment and technology, which may be unaffordable for most injured individuals globally. However, much of the improvement in patient outcomes in these countries has resulted from better organization of trauma care services. This approach is cost-effective and achievable in nearly all settings, forming the basis of the Essential Trauma Care Project. The project identifies deficiencies in trauma care resources and organization that can be addressed through inexpensive measures. These include optimizing the training of medical and nursing staff for trauma care, particularly in rural areas, and ensuring the availability and maintenance of essential equipment. For example, hospitals in rural Ghana often lack staff with specific trauma care training, and 30% of general practitioners in these hospitals have not undergone surgical rotations during their training. Solutions include encouraging experienced trauma care staff to work in such hospitals and providing continuing education courses on trauma care. Many hospitals lack critical equipment for treating life-threatening injuries, such as chest injuries and airway obstructions, despite the affordability and reusability of such equipment. The absence of these resources is often due to poor organization and planning rather than financial constraints. For instance, in Mexico, the lack of repair capabilities for a single CT scanner at a major urban trauma center led to prolonged breakdowns, impairing care for head-injured patients. Programs to ensure the supply and maintenance of trauma-related equipment, tailored to the specific circumstances of each country, could address these deficiencies. Improved administration and organization can also enhance the utilization of available resources. For example, a study in Ghana revealed significant delays in emergency surgery and underutilization of chest tubes, despite their availability. Basic quality improvement programs, such as medical audits, could address these issues simultaneously. The Essential Trauma Care Project builds on existing foundations, including essential health service programs for other diseases and efforts to improve trauma care in individual countries. Examples of essential service programs include the Essential Drugs Programme, the Expanded Programme on Immunization, the Global Tuberculosis Programme, and the Safe Motherhood Initiative. Efforts to improve trauma care in individual countries, such as the American College of Surgeons' Advanced Trauma Life Support (ATLS) course and the publication of Resources for Optimal Care of the Injured Patient, have significantly advanced trauma care in high-income countries. Similar measures have been successfully implemented in other high-income countries, addressing the entire spectrum of trauma management systems. The project emphasizes the importance of planning systems for trauma management, including designating hospitals as trauma centers at varying levels of complexity and organizing mobile emergency medical services and pre-hospital triage. It also highlights the need for capable individuals dedicated to reducing the burden of injury through planning, administration, and clinical services. The Essential Trauma Care Project and its manual aim to support and reinforce these efforts, demonstrating that improved organization of trauma care services can be a cost-effective way to enhance care for injured individuals worldwide.
